newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal truck fleet paralysed by French strike.
newsitem.headline: Portugal truck fleet paralysed by French strike.

text.p: A French truck drivers' strike has paralysed Portugal's road transport fleet which exports and imports vital produce, officials said on Friday.

Carlos Cazenave, secretary-general of the National Association for the Transport of Goods by Road, told Reuters that some 2,000 Portuguese trucks -- about 40 percent of the national fleet -- were now stuck in France.
"From today some 85 to 90 percent of the Portuguese road transport fleet is paralysed because trucks cannot get through France to their destinations across Europe," he said.
"The only business that is proceeding normally is transport of goods between Portugal and Spain," he added.
"We (the association) are putting pressure on the Portuguese government to intervene with the French authorities to try and stop this strike," he said.
Cazenave said the import and export of all kinds of produce ranging from machinery parts to shoes, textiles to electronics equipment and food, were delayed by the French strike.
The French drivers were on strike for a fifth day on Friday, blocking roads and petrol depots around the country in a conflict showing increasing signs of squeezing the economy.
The truckers are demanding wage rises, shorter working hours and retirement at 55 instead of 60.

"It is not right that such a protest in France, which concerns the living standards of French truckers, should affect other countries," said Jorge Neves da Silva, secretary-general of the National Association of Companies in the Car Trade.
"We (in Portugal) have nothing to do with the complaints of the French truckers," he told Reuters.
He said the strike in France had disrupted the import and export of car components to and from Portuguese plants.
Spokesmen at Renault and the Ford-Volkswagen AutoEuropa joint venture in Portugal were not immediately available.
But a spokesman at Siemens said the strike had delayed the export by road of wire cables from the German group's plants in Portugal to a Renault factory in Paris which manufactured Megane cars.
"We have two trucks stuck in Bordeaux since Monday and four more now delayed at the border with France," Hans Muller said.
"If the trucks cannot get through by next Monday, we will charter a plane to get the wire cables through," he added.
"This is more expensive, but we will have to do so to honour our contract."
Muller said that, under a contract between Siemens and Renault, Siemens would be liable to pay a fine if it failed to deliver components on time.
